processing: A pan-fired green taken through fixing, cooling, rolling, second firing, re-rolling, third firing and baking, then sorted and given a final drying. The repeated firing and rolling soften the leaf and form its strip.
harvest_season: Tender shoots picked in the weeks either side of Qingming, mainly one bud and one leaf.
appearance_dry: Straight to slightly curved, sturdy, thick buds covered in snow-white down.
appearance_liquor: Pale green to yellow-green, clear and bright.
taste_profile: Fresh and rich with a high lasting aroma and a sweet return.

brewing.notes: General advice for downy greens: cooled water and an open vessel. Downy tea can look a little hazy, which is not a fault.

vintage_note: Sold as a current-year spring green, as usual for its class, with picking around Qingming. Buy the newest harvest and keep it sealed and cool; it is not a tea to age.
description:
Qingcheng Xueya, snow bud, is the signature green of Qingcheng Shan near Dujiangyan in Sichuan. The name comes from the white down that covers its sturdy buds, and despite the mountain's long tea history the tea itself is a 20th-century creation.

It is made with shoots from around Qingming, mostly one bud and one leaf, and goes through three firings with rollings in between before baking and a final drying. That long sequence softens the leaf and shapes a straight or slightly curved strip while keeping the down.

Expect a high fragrance, a fresh and fairly rich taste, and a sweet finish in a clear pale cup. Use water off the boil and don't panic over a bit of haze; that is the down.

The mountain also produces other teas, including Dujiang Maoting and Qingcheng Gongcha, so check the name. Look for plenty of white down and a current spring harvest.
history:
The tea draws on an old name. Qingcheng tea appears in Lu Yu's Classic of Tea and in Mao Wenxi's Chapu, and the mountain had tea farms from the Song dynasty, but none of that describes this tea as made today.

It was created in the 1950s; the Guan County tea factory is credited with making it in 1959, and the older county name is why it appears under Guanxian in earlier writing. Other teas followed from the same area in the 1980s, the same decade Xueya was rated a famous tea of Sichuan.
